title: Legacy of Fire
description: U.S. Air Force Staff Sgt. Quentin McCray, 436th Civil Engineer Squadron fire station captain, Airman Nathaniel Westberg, 436th CES firefighter and Thomas Krass, 436th CES fire chief, discuss the legacy of the Fire House at Dover Air Force Base, Delaware, April 17, 2025. The three Team Dover members discuss different aspects of the firefighter life and share their personal stories during their time at Dover AFB. (U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Liberty Matthews)
keywords: Dover Air Force Base, fire and emergency services, 436th Civil Engineer Squadron

transcript.text: Our purpose here is to provide
professionalism , duty , and courage to
the citizens of not only Dover , the
city of Dover , but also Dover Air
Force Base and to protect these
aircraft . Airplanes cannot take off
without having the fire department here ,
um , so we give that pilot a sense of
security knowing that if he has an
in-flight emergency or ground emergency
that that aircraft is going to be
protected and we can get it back up and
flying . It's a really big deal
carrying tradition to me . I grew up
around the firehouse . My dad was a
firefighter for most of my childhood ,
being here , kind of continuing on what
he taught me and my dad was a civilian
fire , so getting to do what he was
doing , but serving in the military is
also a really great honor . I think
the biggest thing I've taken away is
that I'm . Capable of a lot by myself
but not nearly as much as with a truck
full of guys . A lot of the guys here ,
even when I just arrived here , it was
first shift . They were already
training me , showing me exactly how to
do how they do it and everything . When
you're on a fire ground , you can't do
it alone . You need someone to pump the
hose . You need someone to drive the
truck . You need someone to call the
shots , whether it's in command , and
then you just need the basic
firefighters to go in and actually
fight the fire or force the door or
rescue the victim or whatever the case
may be . At the end of the day I'm a
family man and um I think that's what
the fire department has instilled in me
is you have to take care of your
responsibilities both here and away . I
was troubled when I came in as a young
airman , not understanding the role of
being a fireman , being away from the
house , and um the one thing I wish I
would have looked back on is , you know ,
talking , let them in , let them know
how your day is going , seeing if uh
you can catch that quick couple minutes
of downtime and you know , reset
yourself . I think the best way to do
that is just to stay grounded and
understand like , hey . Um , I , I am
supporting , um , the people of Dover ,
but I'm also supporting my family , and ,
um , that's what's gonna keep me
motivated when those tough times arise ,
so just being open and having
communication . Within the last
2 years we lost a firefighter here . I
think that not everybody here has been
here for 2 years since he's passed ,
but I think it's caused us to be a lot
more direct with conversations , a lot
more caring . Tomorrow's not promised ,
so you really want to make sure that
you let people know how you're feeling
and not really hold back and to make
sure that people understand you're
there and you care for them .
So as I look back on my time and when I
someday transition out , I don't think
it's about any one person . I think
it's about the team . The only thing I
ask and I and I tell the guys as they
come in , did you leave this fire
department better when you left ? So as
long as we're moving forward in
constant self-improvement , is this
fire department better a year from now ,
5 years from now , 10 years from now
because you were a part of it ? What
did you do ? Small , medium , or large
things to make this department better ?
